12801.title: Exploratory Storytelling
12801.heading: Exploratory Storytelling
12801.content:
Exploratory storytelling distributes optional narrative material through a game space. Players may discover books, objects, conversations, environmental clues, or other fragments while deciding how thoroughly to investigate.

Because these elements can be missed, they usually deepen setting, character, or backstory rather than carry every necessary plot event. Their optional nature makes the player's route and attention part of how the authored material is experienced.

12804.title: Exploratory Regression
12804.heading: Exploratory Regression
12804.content:
Exploratory regression searches for a useful predictive or descriptive model without treating one prespecified exposure–outcome hypothesis as the sole target. Candidate variables may be compared for their contribution to fit or prediction.

Exploration is legitimate when it is labeled and validated as such. Presenting a model discovered through extensive searching as if it tested an a priori hypothesis understates [[Researcher Degrees of Freedom]] and inflates confidence in chance findings.

12807.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
12807.heading: Exploratory Data Analysis
12807.content:
Exploratory data analysis uses summaries and visual displays to investigate distributions, relationships, anomalies, and plausible structures before formal modeling. Scatterplots and multidimensional views often reveal information that a table of statistics conceals.

Exploration should occur throughout knowledge discovery. It helps select attributes and methods, diagnose model behavior, and communicate why a discovered pattern deserves further testing.

12810.sourceSearchName: exploration exploitation tradeoff exploration exploitation tradeoff
12810.title: Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff
12810.heading: Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff
12810.content:
The exploration-exploitation tradeoff is the choice between trying an uncertain action to learn more and selecting the action currently believed to yield the best reward. Too little exploration can trap a learner in a poor policy; too much can degrade performance.

The tension is central to [[Reinforcement Learning]]. For assistants, exploration is especially constrained because a novel dialog action can frustrate a user or produce an unsafe service outcome.

12813.title: Explicit Function Return
12813.heading: Explicit Function Return
12813.content:
An explicit function return uses `return()` to stop execution and deliver a value. It is useful for early exits or when several branches should make their result unmistakable.

The returned object should follow a consistent structure across branches so callers do not need to guess its type.

12816.title: Explicit Challenge
12816.heading: Explicit Challenge
12816.content:
An explicit challenge is one the game states directly to the player. Victory conditions, mission objectives, and immediate instructions commonly make a desired outcome unambiguous.

Explicitness helps players plan, but it does not require explaining the solution. The interface should distinguish the goal from optional guidance and from the actions available to pursue it.

12819.title: Explainable AI
12819.heading: Explainable AI
12819.content:
Explainable AI develops methods and practices that make an automated result intelligible to people. An explanation may identify influential evidence, describe the model's general logic, show why one outcome occurred instead of another, or state how human choices shaped the system.

Explanation is not identical to complete technical disclosure. Different audiences need different answers, and a simplified explanation can mislead if it hides uncertainty or important limitations. Explainability may also trade off against model performance in some designs. Ethical use asks what level of understanding is necessary for informed action, challenge, and [[Algorithmic Accountability]].

12822.title: Expert System
12822.heading: Expert System
12822.content:
An expert system represents domain knowledge explicitly as facts and rules, then applies an inference procedure to reach conclusions. Its two central parts are a knowledge base and an inference engine.

This approach works when experts can enumerate stable rules, but it scales poorly to speech and language because acoustic and linguistic variation creates too many exceptions. [[Machine Learning]] instead learns regularities from examples.

12825.title: Experimental Unit
12825.heading: Experimental Unit
12825.content:
An experimental unit is the entity to which a condition is applied and from which an outcome measurement is obtained. In the source's diet example, each mouse is an experimental unit and contributes one row to the [[Design Matrix]].

Correct identification matters for independence and sample size. Several measurements from one unit are not automatically several independent units, even when they occupy separate data records.

12827.title: Experienced Player Playtest
12827.heading: Document

12828.sourceSearchName: experienced player playtest experienced player playtest
12828.title: Experienced Player Playtest
12828.heading: Experienced Player Playtest
12828.content:
An experienced-player playtest examines the game after participants have learned its basics over repeated or extended sessions. It exposes long-term strategy, progression, balance, repetition, exploits, and whether early interest develops into sustained engagement.

These tests answer different questions from first-use sessions. A design may onboard clearly yet become shallow, or initially confuse players while supporting rich mastery later.

12831.sourceSearchName: experience based play experience based play
12831.title: Experience-Based Play
12831.heading: Experience-Based Play
12831.content:
Experience-based play makes encountering a designed situation more important than winning or mastering a difficult action. Its value may come from exploration, the unfolding of a story, contemplation, or communal participation.

Removing a conventional victory condition does not remove design. The designer still structures attention, pacing, interpretation, and available movement so that players can discover the intended qualities of the experience.

12834.title: Experience Point
12834.heading: Experience Point
12834.content:
An experience point is a numerical marker of progress toward a threshold, commonly a new level. Unlike an expendable [[Game Currency|currency]], experience points are usually accumulated automatically and converted by the system when the threshold is reached.

Crossing that threshold may grant resources, new [[Game Verb|verbs]], or access to new areas. The points therefore represent progress toward a later [[Systemic Reward]] rather than a flexible resource the player can spend immediately.

12837.title: Experience Curve
12837.heading: Experience Curve
12837.content:
The experience curve describes the tendency for the real cost of producing a product or service to decline as cumulative experience doubles. Learning, standardization, scale, and innovation allow the same result to be produced with less expense or effort.

For cloud services, increasing provider and consumer experience can reduce both service costs and the technical skill or time required to use a capability. Different services follow different rates of improvement, so the effect should not be treated as one universal percentage.

An experience design value states the central activity available to the player and the physical or emotional quality that activity should produce. It answers both what the player gets to do and what doing it should feel like.

This value keeps the project centered on play rather than its feature inventory. Two implementations can contain similar mechanics yet support different experiences through timing, framing, feedback, and consequence.

12843.title: Expected Support
12843.heading: Expected Support
12843.content:
Expected support is the sum of the probabilities that an itemset occurs across uncertain transactions. It generalizes deterministic support when individual items are present only with stated probabilities.

An itemset is expected-frequent when this value reaches the threshold. The expectation is efficient to calculate under the model's independence assumptions but does not express the full probability distribution of support.

12846.title: Expected Model Change
12846.heading: Expected Model Change
12846.content:
Expected model change selects the unlabeled case whose possible label would produce the largest anticipated update to model parameters. Because the true label is unknown, the change is averaged or bounded across label possibilities using current predictions.

This criterion favors cases capable of moving the decision function, not merely cases with uncertain outputs. Parameter scale and model geometry determine how update magnitude should be measured.

12849.title: Expected Error Reduction
12849.heading: Expected Error Reduction
12849.content:
Expected error reduction evaluates how much labeling a candidate is predicted to lower future generalization error. For each possible label, the learner estimates the retrained model's error and weights that result by the current label probability.

The criterion targets the final objective directly, but simulated retraining and evaluation make it computationally expensive. Approximation is often necessary when the unlabeled pool or model is large.

12852.title: Expectation-Maximization for Clustering
12852.heading: Expectation-Maximization for Clustering
12852.content:
Expectation-maximization for clustering alternates between estimating probabilistic component memberships from current parameters and updating the component parameters from those weighted assignments.

Each iteration does not decrease the likelihood, but the algorithm normally reaches a local rather than guaranteed global maximum. Hierarchical model-based clustering can provide an initialization.

12855.title: Expectation-Maximization Algorithm
12855.heading: Expectation-Maximization Algorithm
12855.content:
The expectation-maximization algorithm estimates parameters when some variables are unobserved or data is incomplete. It alternates between estimating a distribution over latent values and improving parameters using that estimate.

Each iteration does not decrease the data likelihood, but convergence can lead to a local rather than global optimum. Initialization and model structure therefore influence the learned result.

12858.title: Expectation Step
12858.heading: Expectation Step
12858.content:
The expectation step of expectation-maximization computes the posterior distribution of latent variables using the current parameter estimates. It uses observed data to assign probabilistic responsibility to the missing alternatives.

These expected latent assignments replace unavailable complete-data counts or values in the next optimization. Uncertainty is retained through weights rather than a forced single completion.

12861.heading: Expansion-Reduction Feature Engineering
12861.content:
Expansion-reduction feature engineering first generates a broad collection of transformed variables and then removes weak or redundant candidates. Expansion increases representational possibilities; reduction controls dimensionality and overfitting.

The approach is simple and parallelizable, but exhaustive expansion becomes infeasible with many functions or composition levels. Guided generation and early filtering are therefore central to scale.

12864.title: Existential Quantifier
12864.heading: Existential Quantifier
12864.content:
The existential quantifier ∃ turns an open statement P(x) into the proposition ∃x P(x), which is true when at least one entity in the domain of discourse makes P true.

Negating an existential claim produces a universal denial: ¬∃x P(x) is [[Logically Equivalent]] to ∀x ¬P(x). An existence claim requires only one witness, whereas its negation must rule out every candidate.

12867.title: EXIF Metadata
12867.heading: EXIF Metadata
12867.content:
EXIF metadata use the Exchangeable Image File Format to record camera-generated information within an image file. Common fields include device identity, aperture, shutter speed, ISO, focal length, time, orientation, GPS location, and details of any software that last saved the image.

An analyst can compare these fields with visible properties such as depth of field, motion blur, illumination, or claimed location. Missing EXIF data are common after export or online sharing, so absence alone is not evidence of manipulation.

12870.sourceSearchName: exif image file directory exif image file directory
12870.title: EXIF Image File Directory
12870.heading: EXIF Image File Directory
12870.content:
An EXIF image file directory groups related metadata fields within a JPEG or TIFF structure. Typical directories describe the primary image, camera and exposure information, interoperability fields, the embedded thumbnail, and GPS coordinates.

The directory structure matters because metadata are not merely a flat list of labels. Fields can point to related records and previews, allowing an analyst to compare values produced at different stages of capture and storage. Broken relationships or incompatible entries can indicate that a file was altered or rebuilt by other software.

12873.title: Exhaust Data
12873.heading: Exhaust Data
12873.content:
Exhaust data are traces generated as a by-product of a primary activity rather than gathered chiefly for analysis. Application logs, network traffic, website activity, and sensor streams can add signals that operational transaction systems did not capture explicitly.

Their volume does not imply analytical value. The traces may be low-density, inconsistent, or difficult to integrate with structured records. They may also disclose sensitive behavior despite seeming indirect. A project should ask what these traces represent, how they were produced, and whether their use is appropriate before modeling them.

12876.title: Exergy Efficiency
12876.heading: Exergy Efficiency
12876.content: Exergy efficiency compares useful-product [[Exergy]] with the exergy entering a system: $\epsilon=E_{useful}/E_{in}=1-E_{destroyed}/E_{in}$. It is a second-law performance measure because it tracks whether energy quality survives conversion, not merely whether heat or electrical energy is accounted for. A device may have respectable energy efficiency yet low exergy efficiency when it delivers heat at a temperature poorly matched to its source.

12879.title: Exergy
12879.heading: Exergy
12879.content: Exergy describes the usable quality of an energy flow relative to an environment, rather than only its energy quantity. As irreversibility raises entropy, some ability to produce useful work is lost even if energy is conserved. The source uses exergy analysis to locate losses in conversion systems and to compare a low-temperature solar heater with higher-temperature equipment chosen for power production.

12882.title: Exergy Destruction
12882.heading: Exergy Destruction
12882.content: Exergy destruction is the portion of incoming [[Exergy]] that does not appear in a useful product because of irreversible processes or losses. The source writes a balance as input exergy equals useful-product exergy plus destroyed or lost exergy. Locating that term in a collector, heat exchanger, or power stage shows where design changes can preserve more energy quality, even when a first-law energy balance already closes.

12884.title: Execution-Order Prefix

12885.sourceSearchName: execution order prefix execution order prefix
12885.title: Execution-Order Prefix
12885.heading: Execution-Order Prefix
12885.content:
An execution-order prefix is a numerical code placed at the beginning of a script filename so files sort in the sequence they should run. Leaving gaps between numbers permits later insertion of an intermediate step without renaming the entire workflow.

Prefixes turn a folder of scripts into a visible pipeline. They also help collaborators distinguish preprocessing, data editing, analysis, and exploratory work when the naming convention reserves different number ranges for different kinds of operations.

12888.title: Exclusionary Game Material
12888.heading: Exclusionary Game Material
12888.content:
Exclusionary game material is content or a feature that drives away people who might otherwise enjoy the game's central activity. Unnecessary stereotypes, hostility, sexualization, confusing conventions, or incompatible side content can narrow the audience without strengthening the premise.

The test is not whether any person could object. It is whether the material undermines the experience for the intended audience while contributing little to the design.

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Homological Algebra and Derived Functors]]

12897.title: Exact Complex
12897.heading: Exact Complex
12897.content:
A complex is exact at degree n when the image of the incoming differential equals the kernel of the outgoing differential. It is an exact complex when this holds at every degree.

Equivalently, every [[Homology Group]] of a chain complex vanishes. Exactness says that every cycle is already a boundary, so the complex contains no residual homological obstruction.

12899.title: Exact Sequence
12899.heading: Document
12899.content:
2026-09-13 19:55

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Module Structure and Exact Sequences]]

12900.title: Exact Sequence
12900.heading: Exact Sequence
12900.content:
A sequence of modules and homomorphisms is exact at a module when the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map. It is exact when this equality holds at every position.

Exactness records both what enters and what becomes zero. It is stronger than merely requiring consecutive maps to compose to zero and is preserved by operations such as module localization.

12903.sourceSearchName: exact bayesian inference exact bayesian inference
12903.title: Exact Bayesian Inference
12903.heading: Exact Bayesian Inference
12903.content:
Exact Bayesian inference computes the requested posterior without deliberately approximating its probability values. It applies symbolic transformations or exhaustive numerical operations implied by the model's decomposition.

Exactness can be practical when conditional independences keep intermediate distributions small. Densely connected models or many free variables can make the required sums and integrals prohibitively expensive.

12909.title: Evolving Data Stream Classifier
12909.heading: Evolving Data Stream Classifier
12909.content:
An evolving data stream classifier adapts when the relationship between features and labels changes over time. Recent examples must influence the model more strongly when older patterns no longer describe the current process.

Adaptation can use sliding windows, fading weights, change detectors, or replacement of model components. A learner that adapts too slowly preserves stale concepts, while one that adapts too quickly mistakes random variation for genuine drift.

12912.sourceSearchName: evolution centric feature engineering evolution centric feature engineering
12912.title: Evolution-Centric Feature Engineering
12912.heading: Evolution-Centric Feature Engineering
12912.content:
Evolution-centric feature engineering maintains populations of feature constructions and improves them through operations such as mutation, recombination, and selection. Candidate fitness is based on predictive or representational utility.

Evolution explores irregular combinations that a fixed greedy order might miss. It can also consume many model evaluations, and its results depend on the representation, operators, population diversity, and fitness estimate.

12913.title: Evolution-Centric Feature Engineering

12915.title: Evidence
12915.heading: Evidence
12915.content:
Evidence is the set of variable values treated as known when a probabilistic question is instantiated. Conditioning on that information restricts inference to joint assignments compatible with the observation.

In Bayes theorem, the evidence probability also serves as the normalization across competing hypotheses. Evidence may be hard, fixing a value, or soft, supplying a distribution that expresses uncertain observation.

12917.sourceSearchName: evidentiary data quality evidentiary data quality
12917.title: Evidentiary Data Quality
12917.heading: Document

12918.sourceSearchName: evidentiary data quality evidentiary data quality
12918.title: Evidentiary Data Quality
12918.heading: Evidentiary Data Quality
12918.content:
Evidentiary data quality is the fitness of information to support a claim, finding, or legal decision. It includes accuracy, provenance, relevance, completeness, and the ability to explain how the record was created and transformed.

An automated output is not self-validating merely because it is quantitative. Its weight depends on the quality of the underlying observations and on whether the processing preserves the meaning required by the decision.

12919.sourceSearchName: evidentiary data quality evidentiary data quality
12919.title: Evidentiary Data Quality
12919.heading: References

12920.sourceSearchName: evidence based decision making evidence based decision making
12920.title: Evidence-Based Decision Making
12920.heading: Document

12921.sourceSearchName: evidence based decision making evidence based decision making
12921.title: Evidence-Based Decision Making
12921.heading: Evidence-Based Decision Making
12921.content:
Evidence-based decision making uses systematically collected and analyzed information to support a choice. In a big-data setting, the evidence emerges through a chain of extraction, transformation, integration, cleaning, storage, exploration, and presentation.

A large dataset does not make a decision evidence based by itself. The information must be relevant and trustworthy, and analytical results must be incorporated into the actual decision process.

12924.title: Eventual Consistency
12924.heading: Eventual Consistency
12924.content:
Eventual consistency means that a read model may temporarily lag behind committed source changes but is expected to converge after updates propagate. In a split command-and-query system, a successful write can precede the corresponding read projection, so a user may briefly see the old value. The application must make that delay acceptable through workflow design, status reporting, or a stronger consistency path for operations that cannot tolerate stale reads.

In an event-sourced system, the event stream is updated before asynchronous [[Projection]]s consume the new event. The consistency delay is therefore the interval between appending the event and updating every affected [[Read Model]]. Reliable subscriptions, retries, and [[Projection Checkpoint]]s make convergence possible, while the interface must not promise immediate visibility it cannot provide.

12927.heading: EventStorming Workshop
12927.content: An EventStorming workshop brings domain experts and people who will build the solution into one active modeling session. It needs a large continuous surface, abundant notes and pens, a visible color convention, and enough room for participants to move. The session should favor discovery over presentation: people write and place facts themselves, compare competing flows, and leave unresolved questions as [[EventStorming Hotspot]]s. Its model can later guide deeper workshops, prototypes, and context analysis.

12930.heading: EventStorming Participant Mix
12930.content: An EventStorming participant mix combines people who know how the business operates with people who will design and implement the software. Multiple experts are valuable because knowledge may be fragmented or contradictory, and people from adjacent functions can expose handoffs that one group overlooks. Too homogeneous a group merely repeats its existing assumptions. [[Parallel Event Modeling]] lets specialized participants contribute simultaneously while the shared wall reveals where their event clusters connect.

12933.title: EventStorming
12933.heading: EventStorming
12933.content: EventStorming is a collaborative modeling technique that visualizes how a business behaves using a large surface and color-coded notes. Participants begin with [[Domain Event]]s and arrange them along an [[Event Timeline]], allowing many people to contribute simultaneously. The visible model exposes ambiguous terminology, missing steps, disagreements, and boundaries that a verbal meeting can hide. Its primary output is shared understanding, not a permanent diagram or a mechanically generated implementation.

12935.sourceSearchName: event storming visualization event storming visualization

12936.sourceSearchName: event storming visualization event storming visualization
12936.title: EventStorming Visualization
12936.heading: EventStorming Visualization
12936.content: EventStorming visualization assigns stable colors and shapes to modeling concepts so everyone can interpret the wall consistently. Orange notes represent [[Domain Event]]s, and other colors distinguish uncertainties or outside systems. Once an idea is visible, participants can point to it, move it, question it, or add alternatives instead of relying on different private interpretations of spoken words. The notation should remain simple enough for domain experts to use without learning a technical diagramming language.

12939.title: EventStorming Hotspot
12939.heading: EventStorming Hotspot
12939.content: An EventStorming hotspot marks uncertainty, conflict, or missing information that the workshop cannot resolve productively at that moment. A bright note makes the issue conspicuous without forcing participants to settle it through speculation. This lets the group continue mapping the wider process while preserving a concrete follow-up question. A wall containing many hotspots is not a failed model; it is evidence that the workshop exposed areas where further [[Knowledge Crunching]] is needed.

12942.content: An EventStorming external system represents an organization or technical system outside the modeled team's control. It can receive [[Domain Event]]s or produce events that enter the modeled flow, so placing it on the wall makes integration boundaries and dependencies visible. The notation prevents an outside response from being treated as an internal method call whose timing and reliability are guaranteed. It also helps distinguish the team's model from the broader system in which it participates.

When a new group hesitates, the facilitator can place an initial event to demonstrate the action and invite correction. The facilitator watches time and energy, reinforces consistent colors, and marks unresolved disagreements as [[EventStorming Hotspot]]s rather than deciding domain questions personally. The role enables discovery; it does not make the facilitator the owner of the model.

12948.content: Event-driven architecture reacts to facts that have occurred, such as a customer being created or an order being placed. A producer publishes the event without calling each consumer directly, allowing independently deployed services to respond through messaging. This loose coupling supports scale and change, but event meaning, delivery, ordering, retries, and consistency become explicit service contracts.

12951.heading: Event-Based Input System
12951.content:
An event-based input system converts device-specific changes into named gameplay actions and dispatches them to interested systems. Gameplay code responds to the meaning of an event rather than repeatedly checking particular keys or buttons.

This indirection supports remapping and multiple devices. It also lets different game states subscribe to the actions relevant to them without coupling every object to the hardware interface.

12954.sourceSearchName: event sourced aggregate event sourced aggregate
12954.title: Event-Sourced Aggregate
12954.heading: Event-Sourced Aggregate
12954.content: An event-sourced aggregate records each accepted state transition as one or more [[Domain Event]]s and derives its current state from those events. A command method checks [[Aggregate Invariant]]s, emits an event, and applies it to the in-memory state. Historical events use the same transition logic during [[Aggregate Rehydration]] but are not marked as new changes. The aggregate version advances with applied events and supports [[Optimistic Concurrency]] when new events are appended.

12956.title: Event-Applied State Transition
12956.heading: Document

12957.sourceSearchName: event applied state transition event applied state transition
12957.title: Event-Applied State Transition
12957.heading: Event-Applied State Transition
12957.content: An event-applied state transition changes entity state by first creating a [[Domain Event]] and then applying that event through a dedicated transition function. This couples the fact of change to the state it produces instead of mutating fields and publishing a separate notification that might diverge. Newly raised events are recorded as pending changes, while historical events can use the same transition function during [[Aggregate Rehydration]] without being raised again.

12958.sourceSearchName: event applied state transition event applied state transition
12958.title: Event-Applied State Transition
12958.heading: References

12960.title: Event Upcasting
12960.heading: Event Upcasting
12960.content: Event upcasting enriches a stored event for read-side use by consuming the original event, obtaining additional data, and emitting a new event to a dedicated stream. The upcast event does not replace the aggregate's history; it exists to provide reusable enriched input for one or more [[Projection]]s. Because it adds another subscription and dependency, it is more complex than including stable data in the original event and is justified when several read models need the same enrichment.

12963.title: Event Timeline
12963.heading: Event Timeline
12963.content: An event timeline orders [[Domain Event]]s according to how facts occur in a business process. Sequence shows necessary precedence, while parallel branches show activities that can proceed independently. Building the timeline can reveal that one apparent process crosses several systems or organizational areas. The ordering is a reasoning tool rather than a decorative chronology: participants can ask what happens before, after, or when an expected event fails to occur.

12966.title: Event Stream
12966.heading: Event Stream
12966.content: An event stream is an ordered sequence of events associated with a known identity, commonly one [[Aggregate]] instance. Events must be read in the same strict order in which they were written because replay uses that order to reconstruct state. A stream name can combine the aggregate type and identity. Appending to one stream forms the aggregate's [[Transaction Boundary]], and its revision supplies the expected version for [[Optimistic Concurrency]].

12969.title: Event Sourcing
12969.heading: Event Sourcing
12969.content: Event Sourcing persists the ordered [[Domain Event]]s produced by an aggregate instead of storing only its latest state. To load the aggregate, the application reads its [[Event Stream]] and applies each event through the state-transition function, making history the source of truth. New events are appended after command handling. The approach preserves how a state arose and enables replay, but it requires deliberate event schemas, concurrency checks, [[Projection]]s for queries, and acceptance of [[Eventual Consistency]].

12972.title: Event Store
12972.heading: Event Store
12972.content: An event store is a persistence system designed to append and retrieve ordered events in [[Event Stream]]s. It supports transactional appends, expected stream versions, reading historical slices, and subscriptions for new or existing events. The store preserves the event history used by [[Event Sourcing]]; it is not itself the user-facing query model. [[Projection]]s consume its streams to construct data structures optimized for filtering and display.

12975.sourceSearchName: event aggregator pattern event aggregator pattern
12975.title: Event Aggregator Pattern
12975.heading: Event Aggregator Pattern
12975.content:
An event aggregator receives categorized messages from publishers and forwards them to interested subscribers. Publishers and subscribers do not need direct references to one another, so interface components can react to application events without introducing a web of point-to-point dependencies.

Xamarin.Forms provides `MessagingCenter` as one implementation of this publisher-subscriber arrangement. Message names, payload meanings, subscription lifetime, and unsubscription still need deliberate management because the aggregator hides the direct call path.

12976.sourceSearchName: event aggregator pattern event aggregator pattern
12976.title: Event Aggregator Pattern
12976.heading: References

12978.title: Event Indicator
12978.heading: Event Indicator
12978.content:
An event indicator records whether the outcome occurred within the survival analysis window, commonly as 1 for an event and 0 for censoring. It is interpreted together with the [[Time-to-Event Variable]].

An outcome that occurs after the chosen cutoff is treated as unobserved within that window, even if it is known to happen later. The coding must therefore be regenerated when the study horizon changes.

12990.title: Eulerian Path
12990.heading: Eulerian Path
12990.content:
An Eulerian path is a route through a [[Graph]] that visits every [[Edge]] exactly once. The route need not return to its starting vertex; when it does, it becomes an [[Eulerian Circuit]].

Vertex degrees constrain whether such a path exists. Every intermediate vertex must allow a traveler to enter and leave on different unused edges, so only the starting and ending vertices may have odd [[Vertex Degree]].

12993.content:
Evaluation converts observed play into a diagnosis of why the experience diverged from or fulfilled the design intent. It distinguishes evidence about what happened from a proposed change to the rules, interface, presentation, or content.

A diagnosis should be tested against [[Game Design Values|design values]] and more than one possible remedy. Jumping from a player's symptom to the first suggested feature treats input as an order rather than information for the next iteration.

12996.title: Eulerian Circuit
12996.heading: Eulerian Circuit
12996.content:
An Eulerian circuit is an [[Eulerian Path]] that begins and ends at the same vertex. It is also called an Eulerian tour.

Because the route returns to its start and traverses every edge exactly once, each visited vertex must support paired arrivals and departures. [[Hierholzer's Algorithm]] constructs such a circuit by forming tours from unused edges and splicing them together.

12999.title: Euclidean Algorithm
12999.heading: Euclidean Algorithm
12999.content:
The Euclidean algorithm repeatedly replaces a pair of integers by the divisor and remainder from division. When the remainder reaches zero, the last nonzero remainder is the [[Greatest Common Divisor]].

Working backward expresses that divisor as an integer linear combination of the original numbers.

13002.title: Euler Integration
13002.heading: Euler Integration
13002.content:
Euler integration advances a simulated quantity by adding its current rate multiplied by the time step. In linear motion, acceleration updates velocity and velocity updates position.

The method is simple but accumulates numerical error and can become unstable when the time step varies or grows too large. Physics simulation therefore commonly uses a consistent fixed step even when rendering frames arrive at irregular intervals.

13005.title: Euclidean Distance
13005.heading: Euclidean Distance
13005.content:
Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences between two observations. It corresponds to straight-line distance and produces circular or spherical neighborhoods in ordinary coordinate space.

The measure is sensitive to attribute scale and tends to support compact, globular clusters. Standardization or weighting may be necessary before it expresses the intended resemblance among cases.

The source extends the familiar two-dimensional formula to gene-expression samples with thousands of coordinates. The same square-root sum of squared feature differences defines pairwise sample distance once each column is interpreted as a point in high-dimensional space.

13008.title: Euclidean Inner Product
13008.heading: Euclidean Inner Product
13008.content:
The Euclidean inner product of real coordinate vectors is $u^Tv=\sum_i u_iv_i$. It is the standard dot product.

It produces the Euclidean [[Vector Norm]] and determines the familiar angle and perpendicularity relationships. For complex vectors, the corresponding inner product uses conjugation.

13020.heading: Ethics by Design
13020.content:
Ethics by design integrates ethical requirements into a technology's architecture and development process. Instead of adding a policy statement after completion, a team turns values into choices about data, permissions, constraints, interfaces, logging, testing, and human oversight.

The method can improve [[AI Traceability]], privacy, safety, and accountability, but a value must be interpreted before it can be engineered. Design cannot eliminate conflicts among principles or decide the legitimate purpose of a system by itself. Ethical governance must therefore connect technical features to participation, institutional rules, and the continuing ability to challenge deployment.

13026.title: Escape Velocity
13026.heading: Escape Velocity
13026.content: Escape velocity is the minimum ideal launch speed that lets an object reach indefinitely large distance with no remaining speed under gravity alone. It follows by equating initial kinetic energy with the gravitational potential-energy change and decreases as launch distance from the planet's center increases. For Earth it is about 11.2 kilometers per second near the surface when atmospheric resistance and rotation are neglected.

13029.title: Essential Complexity
13029.heading: Essential Complexity
13029.content: Essential complexity comes from the business problem itself. It cannot be removed without reducing the problem's scope or discarding a rule that matters to the domain. The goal of [[Domain Knowledge]] is not to pretend this complexity does not exist, but to make it explicit enough that a model can protect the right constraints. This differs from [[Accidental Complexity]], which is introduced by the chosen solution and can often be simplified or replaced.

13032.title: Ethernet
13032.heading: Ethernet
13032.content:
Ethernet is a local-area networking method developed by Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox PARC. It lets computers share a communication medium while coordinating transmissions and recovering from collisions.

High local speed allowed workstations to share files, printers, and servers without behaving like dumb terminals. Ethernet helped make client-server computing practical.

13035.title: Ethical Black Box
13035.heading: Ethical Black Box
13035.content:
An ethical black box is a recorder built into an autonomous system to preserve data about its sensors, internal state, decisions, and actions. Like an aircraft recorder, it is intended to help investigators reconstruct what happened after an accident or harmful event.

The device supports [[AI Traceability]] without making the decision model itself fully interpretable. Its ethical effectiveness depends on what it records, how long records are kept, who can access them, and whether the evidence leads to accountability. Recording can also create privacy risks, so the investigation benefit must be designed together with data protection.

13038.content:
Essential boundary condition enforcement prescribes selected nodal unknowns before solving the finite element equations. In structural problems these are imposed displacements; in field problems they may be specified temperatures or potentials.

The elimination method removes the prescribed row and transfers its column contribution to the right-hand side. Penalty and multipoint-constraint methods preserve other useful matrix or relationship structures for software implementation.

13041.title: Error Sum of Squares Clustering
13041.heading: Error Sum of Squares Clustering
13041.content:
Error sum of squares clustering measures the squared deviations of observations from their cluster means. Ward's method chooses each merge to produce the smallest increase in this error.

The criterion rewards compact groups and is affected by measurement scale. Standardizing attributes can materially change the resulting hierarchy.

13044.title: Error Propagation
13044.heading: Error Propagation
13044.content:
Error propagation describes how errors in input values and intermediate operations affect a computed result. Arithmetic may preserve, accumulate, cancel, or magnify those errors.

The algorithm and the underlying problem both matter. Stable procedures limit unnecessary growth, while an [[Ill-Conditioned Linear System]] can magnify even unavoidable small perturbations.

13047.title: Error Checks in Computational Pipelines
13047.heading: Error Checks in Computational Pipelines
13047.content:
Errors can enter a computation while defining the problem, choosing formulas, setting constants, communicating values, storing data, performing operations, or displaying results. A reliable pipeline therefore checks intermediate as well as final outputs.

Checks should be placed where a recipient can verify what it receives before the error propagates. This makes failures easier to localize and prevents a long, fast computation from silently amplifying an early mistake.

13050.title: Error Bar
13050.heading: Error Bar
13050.content: An error bar displays the uncertainty attached to a plotted data point. Horizontal and vertical bars can represent uncertainty in either experimental variable. Their extent helps judge whether a proposed line is consistent with the observations and supports construction of steepest and shallowest plausible gradients rather than treating every plotted coordinate as exact.

13053.title: Equivalent Nodal Load
13053.heading: Equivalent Nodal Load
13053.content:
An equivalent nodal load replaces a distributed or thermal element action with nodal forces that produce the same finite element work. The conversion uses the interpolation model and element geometry.

For a uniformly distributed axial load on a two-node bar, the total is divided consistently between the end nodes. A temperature change produces signed nodal forces governed by modulus, area, and thermal expansion when expansion is constrained.

13056.title: Equivalent Fraction
13056.heading: Equivalent Fraction
13056.content:
Equivalent fractions are different numerator-denominator forms that represent the same number. For a nonzero factor (k),

$$\frac{m}{n}=\frac{mk}{nk}.$$

For example, (2/3=4/6=10/15). Multiplying both components by the same factor changes the partition used to name the point but not the point itself. Dividing both by a common factor reverses the process and leads toward a [[Fraction in Lowest Terms]]. The equality is justified by the [[Cancellation Law for Fractions]].
